notes:
I found good material for vv. 45–46 and 50–53, a little for vv. 54–66, and nothing for vv. 47–49, so those are left out. I couldn't read the full Enduring Word or Pulpit Commentary pages because both cut off before verse 45. Some points therefore come from search excerpts, and a few later-verse notes come from the Spanish version of Guzik's commentary. I found no Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan-site or Pentecostal-site pages on this passage. Some early church writers appear below, but only as other sites quote them.

**v. 45**
- Guzik notes the darkness came at a full moon, when an ordinary eclipse can't happen, and says it mirrored the spiritual agony within Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-27/

**v. 46**
- *Traditional reading:* The cry quotes Psalm 22:1. Bible Hub's notes say that by quoting it, He signals that the entire psalm is being fulfilled in Him—suffering that ends in vindication. They add that Jesus still calls God "My God," which shows trust even in agony. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-46.htm
- Gill: Jesus shows both trust in God and a deep sense of God holding back the comfort of His presence while He bore the wrath due to the sins which he was bearing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-46.html
- Gill also says "forsaken" does not mean the union of His divine and human natures was broken, or that He lost the Father's love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-46.htm
- *Where Protestant teachers differ: how real was the forsakenness?*
  - **Baptist (Piper):** It was a real forsakenness. Jesus was bearing our sin and our judgment. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/my-god-my-god-why-have-you-forsaken-me-didnt-jesus-already-know
  - **Guzik:** Jesus experienced separation from the Father for the first time, carrying God's full wrath against sin in our place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-27/
  - **Matthew Henry:** God forsook Jesus the way He sometimes forsook David (a passing low point), not the way He forsook Saul (endless despair). Though God loved Him as a Son, he frowned upon him as a Surety (one standing in for others). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_027.cfm
  - **Barnes (a softer view):** Jesus was innocent and God approved His work, so God could not have forsaken Him in those senses. Barnes links the cry to His terrible physical suffering and to "the power of darkness" (Luke 22:53). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-46.htm GotQuestions repeats Barnes's caution almost word for word. https://www.gotquestions.org/forsaken-me.html
- *Debated popular teaching:* Some early Word of Faith teachers said Jesus suffered "spiritual death," went down into hell under Satan's power, and had to be born again. Monergism says Kenneth Hagin taught this and that Kenneth Copeland Ministries still teaches a version of it. Monergism answers that the resurrection proved Jesus' finished victory; it was not His rebirth from bondage to Satan. https://www.monergism.com/word-faith-movement The LCMS (Lutheran) lists the claim that Jesus "died spiritually" among Word of Faith views at odds with historic Christianity. https://files.lcms.org/api/file/preview/A810B65D-D26A-4762-8633-D85070F5E77A
- Watch out: one mainstream site uses similar wording without Word of Faith's other claims. "The Bible Says" (on Blue Letter Bible) states that On the cross, Jesus endured both spiritual and physical death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/mat-27-v46.cfm

**v. 50**
- Guzik: no one took Jesus' life. He "yielded up His spirit," and since He never became a sinner Himself, He could not die unless He gave His life up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-27/
- Matthew Henry: the loud cry shows His life was not forced from Him but freely handed over to the Father. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_027.cfm
- Guzik (Spanish edition), quoting another writer: the early church fathers took the loud cry as proof that Jesus died willingly, not from exhaustion. Some modern commentators think it was the cry of someone dying of a ruptured heart. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/mateo-27/

**v. 51**
- *Traditional reading:* The tear running "top to bottom" shows God did it. No human hand opened access to God. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-51.htm
- Gurtner (Desiring God): the wording points to the inner curtain in front of the Most Holy Place. Once torn, it could no longer do its job of separating people from God. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-veil-was-torn-in-two
- *How different teachers apply it:*
  - **Calvin (Reformed):** The tearing ended the ceremonies of the Old Testament law and opened heaven, so that believers may all be a royal priesthood. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-51.html
  - **Clarke (Methodist):** It meant the dividing line between Jews and Gentiles was gone, and the high priest's privilege of entering God's presence now belongs to everyone. (same page)
  - **Spurgeon (Baptist):** The temple seemed to "tear its garment" in mourning, the way people in the East tore their clothes in grief. The tear is so wide that the chief of sinners may find ample passage. (same page)
  - **Coffman:** He uses the verse against priests hearing confession or granting absolution. (same page) An unnamed sermon quoted on Bible Hub likewise sees in it a charter for the priesthood of all believers and a warning against bringing priestly ideas back into the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-51.htm
  - **Barnes:** He urges caution, saying Scripture doesn't explain what the tearing was meant to show. (same page)
- *Modern scholarship:* A Themelios article (on TGC) surveys many views. Origen read it morally, as a call to fear God. T.E. Schmidt saw it as God's Spirit leaving the Jews. Kingsbury held that Jesus replaces the temple. The article also mentions an LCMS-published (Concordia) work that saw it as a sign of the synagogue ending and the church appearing. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-rending-of-the-veil-matt-2751a-par-a-look-back-and-a-way-forward/

**vv. 52–53** (the most debated verses)
- *Traditional reading:* These were real bodies raised, a first taste of the general resurrection (Isaiah 26:19; Ezekiel 37). https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-52.htm
- *When were they raised?*
  - **Piper:** Read naturally, the raising happens at Jesus' death, and the coming out and entering Jerusalem happen after His resurrection. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/split-rocks-open-tombs-raised-bodies
  - **Lenski (Lutheran):** "After his resurrection" applies only to their appearing in the city. **Fowler** argues it applies to both their rising and their appearing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-52.html
  - **Constable:** All of it happened when Jesus rose. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-53.html
- *Did they die again?*
  - **Matthew Henry** thinks, though it can't be proved, that they rose never to die again and went up to heaven with Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_027.cfm
  - **Constable** suspects a Lazarus-type return to ordinary life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-52.html
  - **Ellicott** points out that Scripture says nothing of their going up to heaven. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-52.htm
- *Modern doubts:* Ellicott notes that some critics treat the story as a mythical addition, or as tombs merely exposed by the earthquake. He himself thinks the "saints" were probably believers in Jesus who had died before the crucifixion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-52.htm
- *Early church (as quoted by Bible Hub):* Ignatius and Irenaeus take them as righteous Israelites, and Chrysostom and Augustine are also quoted. https://biblehub.com/q/How_did_saints_rise_in_Matthew_27_52.htm
- Guzik applies the scene spiritually by quoting Spurgeon: rocky hearts are split open and graves of sin are opened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-27/

**v. 54**
- Gurtner: the centurion receives a revelation of who Jesus truly is, and the wonders that start with the torn curtain bear witness to it. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-veil-was-torn-in-two
- Bible Hub: the risen saints back up the centurion's confession. https://biblehub.com/q/Resurrected_saints_role_in_Matt_27_53.htm

**vv. 55–56**
- Matthew Henry: these women stayed boldly with Christ when the male disciples had deserted Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_027.cfm

**vv. 57–61**
- Guzik (Spanish edition): Joseph's tomb sat near the crucifixion site, a reminder that in God's plan the cross and resurrection power are always closely linked. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/mateo-27/

**vv. 62–66**
- Matthew Henry: the disciples remembered "after three days I will rise" to strengthen their faith, while the enemies remembered it in anger. The same word was life to one group and death to the other. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_027.cfm
- Guzik (Spanish edition): the leaders weren't really afraid of a stolen body, since a corpse would prove nothing. What they feared was the resurrection's power. The guard ended up strengthening the evidence, because an unguarded tomb would have made a theft claim hard to disprove. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/mateo-27/
